analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 a month and ends deductibles and prior authorization for covered insulin.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 2, 2026 with a bipartisan group of 11 cosponsors; the bill was sent to three House committees and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private health plans to cover at least one insulin product of each type and dosage form with no deductible and cost-sharing capped at $35 per 30-day supply, starting in 2028, and to bar prior authorization except for safety reasons. It would extend those protections to high-deductible catastrophic plans before the deductible is met. It would also fund a small public resource center and 24/7 hotline to connect uninsured people with manufacturer assistance programs, and direct the government to fast-track review of biosimilar (generic-like) insulin applications when fewer than three biosimilars compete against a brand-name product.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private or employer health insurance who use insulin: they would pay no more than $35 a month for covered insulin, skip the deductible entirely for those products, and no longer need prior approval to fill a prescription. People on catastrophic plans would get covered insulin before meeting their deductible. Uninsured insulin users would get help finding manufacturer assistance programs through a new hotline.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group and individual health plans to cover at least one insulin product of each type, dosage form, and delivery device with no deductible and cost-sharing of no more than $35 per 30-day supply (or 25% of the net negotiated price, if lower), for plan years starting January 1, 2028.
Bars plans from imposing prior authorization or other medical management requirements on selected insulin products, except where clinically justified for safety or reasonable quantity limits.
Requires catastrophic health plans to cover selected insulin products before the enrollee meets the annual deductible.

Funds a grantee to run a resource center and a 24/7 hotline that helps uninsured people find and enroll in manufacturer and other insulin assistance programs, at $2 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2032.

Directs the FDA to expedite review of biosimilar insulin applications for brand-name products with fewer than three biosimilars on the market once all exclusivity periods have expired at least three years earlier.
Orders a Government Accountability Office study of uninsured people who use insulin, including where they live, why they lack coverage, and their income and demographics.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor group plans would absorb the reduced insulin cost-sharing, likely partly through premiums. Pharmacy benefit managers would be barred from receiving payments above the capped amount on selected insulin products, limiting their revenue on those claims. Brand-name insulin makers would face faster biosimilar competition for products with little generic-like competition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, employers, PBMs, drug makers

drawbacks.text: The protections apply only to 'selected' insulin products — one of each type and dosage form chosen by the plan — not to every insulin a doctor might prescribe, so patients whose specific insulin is not the plan's selected product are not covered by the cap.
The requirements do not begin until plan years starting January 1, 2028, so no insulin user sees any benefit before then.

The bill does nothing to lower insulin prices for the uninsured; it only helps them sign up for manufacturer assistance programs, which can keep patients dependent on list prices and manufacturer goodwill rather than lowering drug prices directly.
Insurers and employers will bear the added cost of the cap, which could show up as modestly higher premiums across all enrollees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly millions of Americans with private insurance who use insulin, a hard $35 monthly cap with no deductible is a real, concrete benefit, and the ban on prior authorization removes a common delay in filling prescriptions. The cost is spread broadly across premium payers, and the design is narrow: it covers only each plan's selected products, kicks in two years after passage, and leaves uninsured patients to manufacturer assistance programs rather than addressing prices directly. On balance a genuine help for insulin users, though not a fix for insulin prices overall.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and split across three House committees, none of which has taken it up, and the bill has sat without action while the session runs toward its January 2027 end.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on September 2, 2026, joined by Reps. Miller-Meeks, Schrier, Bresnahan, and Craig as original sponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce Committees.
Eleven members cosponsored the bill: 8 of 217 House Democrats and 3 of 223 House Republicans.
No committee has scheduled a markup or floor action since referral, and the bill's requirements would not take effect before plan year 2028 in any case.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers, pharmacy benefit managers, and health insurers keep the existing cost-sharing arrangement, and uninsured insulin users continue to face full insulin prices, because nothing in the bill has moved or taken effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, PBMs, and insurers keep the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan but lopsided: 8 of 217 House Democrats and 3 of 223 House Republicans signed on, and the original sponsor list pairs Democrat Diana DeGette with Republicans Miller-Meeks and Bresnahan.

industries.note: The bill forces insurers to cover selected insulin products with no deductible, cost-sharing capped at $35 a month, and no prior authorization, shifting those costs onto plans and the premiums all enrollees pay. Insurers gain nothing in return under this bill.

The bill counts price concessions paid to PBMs when calculating the capped amount and bars plans from paying PBMs more than the cap on selected insulin products, limiting the spread PBMs can keep on those claims.

The cost-sharing cap does not directly cut manufacturers' list prices, and the new resource center steers uninsured patients into manufacturer assistance programs, reinforcing those programs' role. But the bill fast-tracks biosimilar review for insulin products with fewer than three biosimilar competitors, increasing competition pressure on incumbents.
Manufacturers of biosimilar insulin get an expedited FDA review path for products facing inadequate competition, letting cheaper versions reach patients sooner.

analysis.trajectory: With three committee referrals, no scheduled markup, and roughly four months left in the session, the bill would need its primary committee to act quickly to have any chance; the overwhelming majority of bills referred to multiple committees receive no further action, so it is likely to die quietly when the session ends in January 2027.
